narrative.text: Section 1 (Introduction) and Related Literature. Motivates how non-random, nonclassical errors in AI/LLM annotations bias downstream social-science regressions and harm replicability, and contrasts gold-standard validation methods (DSL, PPI, MAR-S) with the proposed DMM framework, which uses three or more imperfect proxies without gold-standard labels. Summarizes three main contributions—replacing gold-standard labels via conditional CP decomposition given the latent label and rich unit covariates, general moment-estimator applicability for categorical independent or dependent variables with J >= 3 proxies, and LLM-specific design and diagnostic strategies—before situating DMM relative to the AI-generated data, repeated-measurement identification (Kruskal, Hu, Allman–Matias–Rhodes, Dawid–Skene), and proxy-based causal inference literatures.

Section 2 opening (The Problem Setting and Existing Approaches). Notes that ignoring measurement error in machine or human annotations biases downstream analysis even when annotation accuracy exceeds 90%, and states that Section 2 and Section 3 first focus on a binary error-prone independent variable before Section 4 generalizes to multicategory independent or dependent variables.

Section 2.1 (Setup). Formalizes the binary latent independent variable setting: for n units with unobserved true label X*_i in {0,1}, observed outcome Y_i, covariates W_i, and J >= 3 binary proxy labels X^(j)_i, the target parameter beta* uniquely solves the full-data moment equation E[psi_F(Y, X*, W; beta)] = 0. Illustrates psi_F for linear, logistic, and generalized linear models and notes that under model misspecification beta* represents the population projection parameter.

Section 2.2.1 (Naive Approaches Ignoring Measurement Errors). Shows that collapsing J proxy labels into a single index X-check (such as majority voting) and plugging it directly into the downstream moment equation yields a population moment bias E[(X-check - X*){psi_F(Y,1,W;beta) - psi_F(Y,0,W;beta)}], which remains nonzero even at high classification accuracy because classification errors are nonclassical and correlated with downstream variables.

Section 2.2.2 (Gold-Standard-Only Estimation). Defines the inverse-probability-weighted gold-standard-only (GSO) estimator using units sampled for expert labeling with known researcher-controlled probabilities rho_i = Pr(R_i = 1 | Y_i, W_i, X-tilde_i). Notes that GSO is consistent and asymptotically normal for beta* but inefficient because it discards the proxy labels and all unlabeled units.

Section 2.2.3 (Debiased Inference with Gold-Standard Labels). Reviews prediction-and-correction estimators (DSL, PPI, MAR-S) that combine large-scale proxy predictions with a gold-standard validation sample, presenting the cross-fitted doubly robust DSL moment function as a benchmark. Explains that DSL achieves unbiasedness for the oracle moment under a known sampling design without assumptions on LLM error structure, and contrasts the continuum of naive, GSO, and validation-based bias-correction approaches.

Closing paragraph of Section 2.2.3 transitioning to Section 3. Observes that validation-based methods such as DSL and PPI require gold-standard labels for a subset of units—which can be prohibitively costly or infeasible—motivating Section 3's gold-standard-free approach.

Section 3 opening and Section 3.1 (Assumptions). Reviews the classical conditional independence assumption X^(1) _||_ ... _||_ X^(J) | X* from the latent-class literature and explains why it fails when human or LLM annotators share input-driven or prompt-driven error sources. Introduces Assumption 3.1, which conditions on both the latent label X* and observed covariates D-tilde = (D, W, Y)—including task features such as text embeddings or prompt metadata—so misclassification rates can vary across both annotators and units.

Section 3.2 opening (Identification overview). Outlines the two-step identification strategy under Assumption 3.1: first identifying each proxy's conditional true- and false-positive rates eta*_{j,a}(d) = Pr(X^(j) = 1 | X* = a, D-tilde = d) via array decomposition, and second constructing an unbiased bridge function H(X-tilde, D-tilde) satisfying E[H | X*, D-tilde] = X* to form the observed-data moment psi_DMM whose expectation matches the oracle full-data moment.

Section 3.2.1 (Identification of Conditional Classification Rates). Adapts Allman, Matias, and Rhodes (2009) Theorem 4 and Kruskal's (1977) uniqueness theorem by partitioning the J >= 3 proxies into three nonempty subsets to form a three-way conditional probability tensor with a two-component CP decomposition. Shows that when each subset contains at least one informative proxy, Kruskal's rank condition k_1 + k_2 + k_3 >= 6 holds with equality, and combining this with an anchoring rule (such as eta*_{j+,1} > eta*_{j+,0}) uniquely identifies the mixing probabilities and all conditional classification rates eta*_{j,a}(d) (Result 1).

Section 3.2.2 (Identification via the Robust Bridge Function). Defines single-proxy bridges M_j = (X^(j) - eta*_{j,0})/(eta*_{j,1} - eta*_{j,0}) and combines pairwise and triplewise averages into the symmetric Neyman-orthogonal robust bridge H^R = 3 H_2 - 2 H_3 using at least three proxies. Proves Proposition 3.1 showing that H^R is unbiased for X* and has only second- and third-order conditional bias in cross-fitted first-stage nuisance errors (yielding O_p(delta_n^2) remainder), and proves Theorem 3.1 establishing identification of beta* via the DMM moment equation.

Section 3.3 (Estimation and Inference). Defines the K-fold cross-fitted DMM estimator beta-hat_DMM using out-of-fold nuisance estimates (e.g., via EM or sieve methods) and proves Theorem 3.2: beta-hat_DMM is consistent when J - 1 proxy nuisance models converge (multiple robustness) and root-n asymptotically normal when nuisance errors converge at rate o_p(n^{-1/4}), with a plug-in sandwich variance estimator. Analyzes asymptotic efficiency as a function of proxy count J and single-bridge variances kappa_{j,a}(d), showing an O(J^{-2}) bridge-variance reduction under homogeneous proxies and noting that adding a very noisy proxy can increase variance unless it passes an explicit variance threshold.

Section 4 opening (Extensions). Outlines the two generalizations of the DMM framework developed in Section 4: binary latent dependent variables (Section 4.1) and multicategory latent independent or dependent variables (Section 4.2).
Section 4.1 (Latent Dependent Variable) heading stub introducing Subsection 4.1.1.

Section 4.1.1 (Setup and Identification for a Latent Dependent Variable). Formulates the binary latent outcome model where Y*_i in {0,1} is unobserved and J >= 3 binary outcome proxies Y^(j)_i are conditionally independent given (Y*, D-tilde) with D-tilde = (D, W) (Assumption 4.1). Constructs the outcome-proxy bridges M^Y_j, the symmetric robust outcome bridge H^R_Y, and the observed-data moment phi^DMM_Y, proving Proposition 4.1 that beta* is identified as the unique root of E[phi^DMM_Y] = 0.

Section 4.1.2 (Estimation and Inference for a Latent Dependent Variable). Defines the cross-fitted estimator beta-hat^DMM_Y and states Theorem 4.1 establishing consistency under o_p(1) nuisance error and root-n asymptotic normality with sandwich variance A_{Y,0}^{-1} Omega_{Y,0} A_{Y,0}^{-T} when the outcome-proxy nuisance estimators converge at rate o_p(n^{-1/4}).

Section 4.2 (Multicategory Labels). Extends DMM to a K*-category latent variable with J >= 3 proxies of potentially differing category counts K_j by defining class-specific bridge functions H_a(Y-tilde, D-tilde) via the left inverse S^+(d) of the conditional measurement matrix S(d) and combining single-proxy bridges into the Neyman-orthogonal robust bridge H^R_a = 3 H_{2,a} - 2 H_{3,a}. Discusses Kruskal rank conditions (3K* >= 2K* + 2 when three proxy groups have full column rank K*), composite proxy grouping when individual proxies have fewer than K* categories, anchoring across all K* classes, and uniform lower bounds on the smallest singular value sigma_min{S_j(d)}.

Section 5 opening (Designing and Assessing Conditional Independence). Emphasizes that conditional independence of measurement errors is a structural assumption not guaranteed by high proxy accuracy, and previews the three parts of Section 5: measurement design (Section 5.1), gold-standard-free diagnostics (Section 5.2), and direct testing plus DMM-assisted DSL bias correction when a small validation sample is available (Section 5.3).

Section 5.1 (Making the Conditional Independence Assumption More Plausible). Recommends three practical strategies for LLM and human annotation designs: (1) enriching the conditioning set D-tilde with input features (text length, style, embeddings, or cross-LLM disagreement scores as task-difficulty proxies); (2) partitioning annotators into G >= 3 conditionally independent groups across distinct model families (e.g., GPT, Claude, open-weight LLMs, and blinded humans) while allowing arbitrary within-group error dependence; and (3) randomizing or recording prompt versions across annotators to prevent prompt-induced error correlation.

Section 5.2 (Diagnostics Without Gold-Standard Labels). Notes that three binary proxies with two latent classes are just-identified (7 degrees of freedom and 7 parameters), whereas J >= 4 proxies yield 2^J - 2J - 2 overidentifying restrictions at each covariate value d. Proposes two gold-standard-free specification diagnostics: goodness-of-fit / conditional moment tests comparing the fitted product-mixture distribution to the empirical joint label distribution, and multiplier-bootstrap stability tests comparing DMM parameter estimates across distinct subsets of three or more proxies.

Section 5.3 (Testing and Bias-Correction with Small Gold-Standard Data). Shows how a small validation sample with known sampling probabilities rho_i enables (1) a direct conditional moment test of zero residual products across proxy subsets given X* = a and D-tilde, and (2) a DMM-assisted DSL estimator that uses the cross-fitted DMM moment function as a full-sample imputation / control variate corrected by inverse-probability-weighted validation residuals, guaranteeing validity even if conditional independence fails while improving precision when DMM is informative.

Section 6 opening (Simulation and Empirical Validation). Previews the two empirical evaluations of DMM: a calibrated simulation study of political advertising tone based on Fowler et al. (2021) where conditional independence holds by construction for a latent dependent variable (Section 6.1), and a real-data validation study of online corruption complaints in China based on Pan and Chen (2018) with LLM proxy annotations for a latent independent variable without imposing conditional independence (Section 6.2).

Section 6.1 (Simulation Study: Platform Differences in Political Advertising Tone). Evaluates DMM over 500 Monte Carlo replications calibrated to 12,973 ads from Fowler et al. (2021), estimating the Facebook coefficient (target 1.314) in a logistic regression for the binary Promote indicator as J increases from 3 to 15 F1-ranked proxies. Reports that with the top 3 proxies naive majority voting suffers severe bias (0.186) and near-zero 95% CI coverage (0.018), whereas DMM eliminates bias (0.002), achieves nominal coverage (0.948), cuts RMSE by two thirds (0.063 vs. 0.191), and approaches the infeasible oracle RMSE (0.045) as informative proxies are added.

Section 6.2 (Empirical Validation: Accusations of Wrongdoing in China) and Figure 1 captions/labels. Evaluates DMM on 1,412 real citizen complaints from Pan and Chen (2018) using three LLM proxies (GPT-4.1 5-shot, GPT-4 5-shot, Llama-4 0-shot) for the latent prefecture-level wrongdoing regressor in a logistic regression of upward reporting (expert benchmark -1.039). Shows that single-proxy naive estimates are heavily biased (-1.869 to -0.388, coverage 0.154-0.572), while DMM without any expert labels yields -0.844 with 0.862 resample coverage, comparable to DSL using 500 expert labels (-1.279, coverage 0.981).

Section 7 (Discussion), Figure 2 labels/caption, and References. Synthesizes DMM's methodological contributions—identifying conditional classification rates via covariate-conditioned latent-class decomposition, achieving Neyman orthogonality and single-proxy misspecification robustness via the symmetric bridge H^R, and analyzing how proxy count and quality govern asymptotic variance—alongside its main limitation (reliance on conditional independence) and complementarity with validation-based methods (DSL, PPI), followed by the full bibliography.

Appendix A opening (Proofs). Sets up K-fold cross-fitting notation, empirical and population expectation operators (P, P_{n,k}, P_n), and shorthand for the fold-specific fitted single-proxy bridges M-hat_{j,-k}, robust bridge H-hat^R_{-k}, and DMM moment function psi_DMM(O; beta, eta) used throughout the technical proofs.

Appendix A.1 (Proof of Proposition 3.1: Bounds for the Robust Bridge). States and proves Lemma A.1 and Proposition 3.1, deriving exact pairwise and triplewise product expansions for the foldwise conditional bridge errors B^R_{1,-k}(D-tilde) and B^R_{0,-k}(D-tilde), proving that linear error terms cancel because 3(2/J) - 2(3/J) = 0, establishing L_2 bounds ||M-hat_{j,-k} - M_{j,0}||_{2,P} <= C delta_n and P|B^R_{a,-k}| <= C delta_n^2, and showing exact zero bridge bias when at most one proxy's nuisance model is misspecified.

Appendix A.2 (Proof of Theorem 3.2: Second-Order Remainder for the DMM Moment Function and Large-Sample Theory). Proves Lemma A.2 bounding the foldwise conditional population remainder ||R_{n,k}(beta)||_2 <= C delta_n^2 uniformly on B_0, and completes the proof of Theorem 3.2: establishes consistency (including multiple robustness when J - 1 proxies are consistently estimated) via an r-net union bound and Z-estimation, proves root-n asymptotic normality when delta_n = o_p(n^{-1/4}) via mean-value expansion and Slutsky's theorem, and verifies consistency of the plug-in sandwich covariance estimator V-hat.

Appendix B (Details for the Efficiency Discussion). Derives the oracle-plus-bridge-noise decomposition of the DMM meat matrix Omega^R_{0,J} (equations 3.17-3.19) and uses conditional orthogonality of centered single-bridge errors epsilon_j to obtain the exact conditional bridge variance formula v^R_{a,J}(d) in terms of elementary symmetric sums S_{1,a,J}, S_{2,a,J}, and S_{3,a,J} of single-proxy variances kappa_{j,a}(d). Derives the exact variance-reduction threshold kappa-bar_{J,a}(d) for adding a (J+1)-th proxy and shows that under homogeneous proxy variance kappa_a(d), v^R_{a,J}(d) decays at rate O(J^{-2}) and any new proxy with variance below asymptotically 2 kappa_a(d) improves precision.

Appendix C opening (Additional Details on the Experiments). Outlines the contents of Appendix C covering the relationship of the two Section 6 empirical exercises to their original studies, the shared low-dimensional logistic latent-class model and EM algorithm, and the application-specific simulation and validation protocols.

Appendix C.1 (Scope and Relationship to the Original Applications). Clarifies how the two Section 6 studies simplify the original empirical specifications to isolate a single latent binary variable: using an ad-level logit on 12,973 complete-case ads without candidate fixed effects for Fowler et al. (2021), and focusing solely on the prefecture-level wrongdoing main effect without county-level wrongdoing interactions on 1,412 complaints for Pan and Chen (2018). Explains the three evaluation roles played by expert labels (oracle benchmark, synthetic DGP calibration, and retrospective F1 ranking of proxy sets).

Appendix C.2 (Model Specification). Specifies the shared parametric logistic latent-class nuisance model used in both applications, modeling latent prevalence Pr(L*_i = 1 | Z_i) = expit(Z_i^T alpha) and class-specific proxy response probabilities Pr(L^(j)_i = 1 | L*_i = a, Z_i) = expit(Z_i^T gamma_{j,a}) without including the downstream outcome Y_i in the Pan-Chen measurement likelihood.

Appendix C.2.1 (Expectation-Maximization Algorithm). Details the E-step log-sum-exp posterior responsibility update xi^(t)_i and M-step fractional/weighted logistic regressions for fitting the latent-class nuisance model, along with Table C.1's shared numerical settings (6 starts, 500 max iterations, 10^{-5} responsibility tolerance, 10^{-7} log-likelihood tolerance, [-20,20] coefficient clipping, [10^{-8}, 1-10^{-8}] probability clipping, and 0.05 bridge denominator floor) and post-EM sign orientation.

Appendix C.2.2 (From the EM Nuisance Fit to DMM). Gives the exact finite-sample implementation formulas for converting EM nuisance fits into the stabilized single-proxy bridges M-hat_{ij} (with denominator floor epsilon = 0.05), the robust bridge H-hat^R_i, the generated-outcome quasi-score equation for the Fowler latent-outcome logit, the weighted moment equation for the Pan-Chen latent-regressor logit, and empirical sandwich standard errors.

Appendix C.3 (Monte Carlo Simulations). Documents the full calibration and evaluation protocol for the Fowler et al. (2021) simulation study (12,973 ads, Promote prevalence 0.756, target Facebook logit coefficient 1.3141, 500 replications per nested proxy count J, random tie-breaking for even-J majority vote) and summarizes additional simulations for the lower-prevalence Contrast (17.2%, target -1.029) and Attack (7.1%, target -1.334) tone indicators.

Appendix C.4 (Empirical Validation) and Tables C.2-C.3. Presents Table C.2 (Fowler simulation results for Attack and Contrast outcomes showing near-zero DMM bias and 0.942-0.962 coverage versus severe naive bias and undercoverage) and Table C.3 (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and weighted/positive F1 for the three LLM proxies in Pan and Chen 2018), and documents the 1,412-complaint logistic specification, the 500-label generalized-random-forest DSL benchmark, and the 500-draw nonparametric bootstrap coverage diagnostic.

Front matter and abstract for Egami and Shin (MIT), 'Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data without Gold-Standard Labels: Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements' (arXiv:2608.18294v2). Treating AI-measured variables as error-free biases downstream inference even above 90% accuracy, while existing corrections (DSL, PPI) require costly gold-standard labels. The authors propose debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements (DMM), which combines three or more error-prone AI annotations under conditional independence given the latent true label and observed unit-level features (such as text embeddings), proves consistency and asymptotic normality via semiparametric inference theory, and introduces diagnostics for the conditional independence assumption.
